claims.text: At street level, look for Anish Kapoor’s mirrored sculpture tucked beneath the projecting corner beside the lobby.

evidence.locator: Architect’s announcement and photographs of the installation

claims.text: Some of the glass façade panels are operable windows. They let residents bring in outside air directly, even high above the street.

evidence.locator: Project description, exposed structural slabs and operable façade units

claims.text: McKim, Mead & White drew on Rome’s Baths of Caracalla for the station’s grand waiting room. The station organized passengers, trains, and street traffic on separate levels.

evidence.locator: Historical information, significance and history of construction

claims.text: In interior photographs, the main waiting room has a heavy coffered vault. The train concourse is recognizable by its tall glazed roof and open steel framing.

evidence.locator: Photographs 6 and 11, main waiting room and train concourse

claims.text: From Broadway, follow the pale terra cotta up to the steep, copper-clad crown. The Gothic ornament becomes denser toward the roof.

evidence.locator: LP-1273, exterior description

claims.text: The lobby’s carved portraits make jokes about the people who built it. Architect Cass Gilbert holds a miniature of his tower, and Frank Woolworth is shown paying for it with nickels and dimes.

evidence.locator: LP-1121, description of lobby arcade and portrait grotesques

claims.text: In old Lower Manhattan photos, look for the tall square shaft rising above a broad base. A mansard roof with large arched openings and a narrow copper lantern topped the tower.

evidence.locator: Architectural information, exterior and roof descriptions

claims.text: The copper lantern originally carried a 60-foot flagpole. By the time surveyors documented the building during demolition, the pole had been removed.

evidence.locator: Architectural information, dormers and towers

claims.text: Look at how the lower edge of the steep roof flares outward over the shingled walls.

evidence.locator: Section 7, description of the roof and walls

claims.text: The federal landmark survey describes the earliest wall framing as filled with wattle and daub, a woven lattice coated with an earthen mixture. The later additions used brick infill.

evidence.locator: Section 7, description of frame construction and infill

claims.text: Inside the former banking hall, a ring of red marble columns frames the central rotunda beneath the dome.

evidence.locator: LP-1908, Main Banking Room description

claims.text: The bank worked its name into the architecture. Enlarged versions of the winged-cap design from the Mercury dime decorate the rotunda’s column capitals.

evidence.locator: LP-1908, description of the rotunda ornament

claims.text: Look for the red-carpeted flight tube that now connects the former terminal lobby with JFK’s Terminal 5.

evidence.locator: Walking directions from JetBlue Terminal 5

claims.text: Early plans called for glass passageways with moving sidewalks. The design team switched to enclosed concrete tubes and dropped the moving walks.

evidence.locator: LP-1916, walkways to the gate structures and note 18

claims.text: In Flushing Meadows, use the Unisphere as your landmark. The long, low museum building stands right beside it.

evidence.locator: 1964 World's Fair section

claims.text: For decades after the 1964 fair, the building had a model of all five boroughs at one end and an ice rink at the other. The museum’s 2013 expansion took over the rink space.

evidence.locator: 1964 World's Fair and 2013 expansion sections

claims.text: The scale is the giveaway. The cottage has three rooms on the ground floor and two tucked into the attic.

evidence.locator: Description of the five-room cottage

claims.text: This small Fordham house is where Poe wrote The Bells, Eureka, and Annabel Lee.

evidence.locator: Account of Poe’s years in the cottage

claims.text: In photos from before the 1970s renovation, look for the scalloped copper frieze that edged the roof over the upper grandstand.

evidence.locator: Opening-day design and 1970s renovation

claims.text: A piece of the original copper frieze survived the renovation. The team’s museum lists it among its stadium artifacts.

evidence.locator: Yankee Stadium exhibits, portion of original copper frieze

claims.text: At the waterfront, look for the Gothic Revival additions, including the decorative wood trim along the gables and the projecting bay window.

evidence.locator: Section 7, Gothic Revival alterations and additions

claims.text: Alice Austen developed her photographs in a second-floor darkroom at Clear Comfort and rinsed them at the pump behind the house.

evidence.locator: Section 8, photography and the house, p. 12

claims.text: From Richmond Terrace, look for paired stairs and doors, with small New York City shields in the door surrounds. The pale cladding is terra cotta finished to resemble limestone.

evidence.locator: LP-2058, Richmond Terrace façade description

claims.text: A parade marked the building’s opening in 1923 as the 66th Precinct station. It became the 120th in 1929 during a citywide precinct renumbering.

evidence.locator: LP-2058, Opening of the Police Station and Subsequent History
